text: In an AI system, each text token begins as a row of numbers called in embedding.
As the AI processes your message, the neural network layers change those numbers to reflect
the surrounding context.
But those new numbers might not match the starting numbers for any token.
How can they still represent meaning?
An exact match isn't necessary.
The relationships between the numbers matter, too.
We can picture those relationships as positions on a map, where nearby positions can represent
similar meanings.
That's the idea behind vector space.
This map of the United States uses two numbers to describe position, latitude and longitude.
Dallas, Texas sits at roughly 33 degrees north, 97 degrees west.
New York City and Mountain View have their own coordinates, using those same two dimensions.
Introducing two new sets of coordinates, we establish location by finding the nearest
match.
38 degrees north, 120 west, connects to Mountain View.
40 degrees north, 76 west, connects to New York City.
When nothing matches exactly, distance finds the closest one.
Their position still tells us which city they're near.
This table applies that exact positional logic to the flavor profiles of drinks.
Instead of two geographic coordinates, each drink gets a row of numbers, called a vector,
describing seven characteristics, from sweet and bitter to citrus.
Looking across the rows, Cokes and Pepsi's numbers are nearly identical, while Coffey's
scores differ in almost every column.
Coke and Pepsi have more similar profiles than either does to Coffey.
Just as latitude and longitude give a city a position, a drink's seven ratings give
it a position in a space with seven dimensions.
That's vector space.
This spatial map plots those seven-dimensional vectors.
Coke and Pepsi score similarly across the board, so they plot right next to each other,
creating a soft drink's neighborhood.
Coffey, with its opposing numeric scores, plots in a completely different area.
The long distance between these sets of data establishes a separate hot drink's
neighborhood.
Now, we introduce a mystery drink with a new set of seven ratings.
To find its identity, we check the distance to our established points,
specifically looking at the citrus column at the far right.
The mystery drink's ratings are closest to Pepsi's.
The first six scores match Pepsi exactly.
Only the citrus score differs.
It's a nine instead of a ten, which is a gap of just one.
Compared to Coke's citrus score of one, the gap is eight.
Smaller gaps mean closer positions.
AI uses this exact mechanism to understand text.
During training, it learns embeddings with thousands of dimensions.
Similar meanings occupy nearby positions in that massive vector space.
This map shows how AI resolves meaning in
the cat sat on the mat during the May rainstorm because it was tired.
On its own, it is completely ambiguous.
As network layers process the sentence,
they update its numbers to connect it to cat.
We trace its physical update path, moving from starting coordinates 0.12,
negative 0.34, directly to 0.41, 0.06.
Its new position reflects its connection to cat.
The updated numbers no longer match the original embedding.
Landing inside the animal's neighborhood perfectly represents the token's updated
meaning based on its geometric relationship to the concepts around it.
Meaning is a position in vector space.
Similar meanings usually sit close together.
